transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02
Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~55m
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Maya (QwestWorks Head ML), Jordan (Infra), Samir (CTO)

Summary: Quick qualification on cost constraints, interest in hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem). Main asks: per-token cost sensitivity at 50k-200k reqs/day; latency SLO ~200-400ms P95 for short responses; ability to run a short benchmark with real payloads.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching and caching levers, KV cache, quantization, burst capacity, SOC2/KMS, pilot scope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sofia from Redwood, i got Ravi our SE as well. um does that sound good?
[00:10] Maya: Yep thanks, I appreciate it. Quick context, QwestWorks builds a real-time summarization layer for customer support... we currently use an internal transformer for rerank + summarize.
[00:22] Samir: We're re-evaluating serving because our TCO doubled last quarter, we're exploring managed hosted but want options for dedicated or VPC because of data residency.
[00:34] Sofia: Great, high level — are you most constrained by raw $/token or by latency/service reliability right now?
[00:41] Jordan: Budget first. If we can't hit a certain cost per 1k tokens we'll probably continue self-hosting. Latency matters but we can tolerate up to ~350ms p95 for the short 128 token responses.
[00:52] Ravi: Helpful. when you say cost per 1k tokens, do you have a target or a current blended number?
[00:57] Maya: Right now around $0.08 per 1k tokens with our infra plus ops. We need to see if Redwood hosted or a dedicated pool moves that to the $0.03-0.05 range ideally.
[01:09] Sofia: okay that gives us a good anchor. We're going to look at two levers: model selection + quantization, and serving optimizations like batching and KV/prefix caching.
[01:21] Maya: Can you walk through how batching reduces per-token cost versus impacting latency? That's the tradeoff we worry about.
[01:27] Ravi: Sure. So continuous batching groups incoming tokens across requests to improve GPU utilization. For short responses batching gives big wins on throughput but can add a small queuing delay. In Redwood Dedicated you can set latency SLOs and a batching profile — we run dynamic batch windows that try to fold very short waits into micro-batches.
[01:47] Ravi: For example, 8ms median added wait might reduce token cost by 30% if you're moving from one request-per-batch to 16 tokens per batch on average. Those numbers are workload dependent.
[01:58] Jordan: That 8ms sounds fine. But during peak bursts we need predictable tail latency. How do we avoid 500-600ms spikes?
[02:05] Ravi: We recommend a hybrid: a small pool with stricter SLOs for latency-critical routes, and a lower-cost pool that accepts higher batching for background/async tasks. Smart routing can failover if the latency pool is saturated.
[02:20] Samir: Do you do prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts? We have a lot of similar context windows across sessions.
[02:26] Ravi: Yes — Redwood has KV cache and prefix caching. If your requests have common prefixes we can cache the KV state so subsequent calls skip early attention computation. That can cut token work significantly, especially for multi-turn flows.
[02:40] Maya: How does that show up in the unit econ? Do you show effective tokens billed or raw?
[02:45] Sofia: Our pricing is per-token generated + context tokens, but the effective cost we report to customers can be reduced because caching means fewer GPU ops. In the pilot spreadsheet we'll show both raw and cache-adjusted token counts.
[02:58] Maya: Okay good. Also curious about private/VPC options — if we need KMS and audit logs, does Redwood Private support HSM-backed keys and full audit trail?
[03:08] Ravi: Yes. Private deployments support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with HSMs. We also expose detailed audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM. SOC2 Type II is available for hosted customers; Private adds more controls for compliance.
[03:22] Jordan: What about model variants — can you fall back to smaller quantized models automatically if the bigger model is saturated?
[03:29] Ravi: Automatic fallback is possible: routing policies can prefer a high-quality model, with fallback to a slightly smaller quantized variant if throughput or cost triggers are hit. That preserves availability while bounding cost.
[03:41] Maya: This is helpful. For the pilot we want to compare: Redwood Hosted (managed), Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool in our cloud account), and Private VPC. We only plan 50k to 200k inference calls per day initially.
[03:52] Sofia: Perfect. To make the pilot meaningful we need a sample token distribution and a few representative prompt templates. Jordan, can you provide a CSV with request counts by prompt and avg token lengths?
[04:03] Jordan: Yep we'll do that. Also, do you support on-prem deployment if we need air-gapped later?
[04:09] Ravi: We have an on-prem package that mirrors Private feature set, yes — it's used by healthcare and finance customers.
[04:15] Samir: Great. A few nitty-gritty questions: burst capacity — can Dedicated autoscale during sudden spikes?
[04:22] Ravi: Dedicated supports burst capacity and configurable autoscaling policies. You can reserve baseline capacity and allow bursts from an overflow pool. There are cost implications; reserved baseline lowers unit cost but burst billed at premium.
[04:34] Maya: We expect a daily pattern with big midday spikes. Our main KPI: keep average cost below $0.05/1k tokens while keeping 95th latency < 400ms.
[04:45] Sofia: Noted. We'll model that in the spreadsheet using your distribution. We'll show hosted vs dedicated vs private with the same workloads and include quantized model options.
[04:55] Maya: On pricing: how granular is the hosted per-token pricing? Is there a commitment discount?
[05:00] Sofia: Hosted is per-token with volume tiers; significant discounts for committed reserved capacity (that's the Dedicated offer). For Dedicated we provide committed monthly spend and lower unit price, plus burst allowances.
[05:11] Jordan: Is there any network egress or hidden cost for VPC/private?
[05:15] Ravi: For Private/VPC, you manage networking — there might be cloud egress costs in your account; Redwood charges platform license for Private but not per-token egress. We'll call those out in the pilot cost sheet.
[05:27] Maya: Okay. Could you outline what the benchmark run looks like? We want to run 3 model sizes and two configs: with and without KV cache and quantized vs fp16.
[05:37] Ravi: That’s reasonable. Plan: 3 models (base, mid, large), seq-length buckets (64/128/512), quantized and fp16 variants, caching enabled/disabled. We'll measure p50/p95 latency and effective token/sec and compute cost per 1k tokens using Redwood's runtime telemetry. We'll run them in hosted and dedicated (if you approve test VMs) to compare.
[05:57] Samir: For dedicated tests, what access do you need? SSH to a bastion?
[06:01] Ravi: We'll need a short-lived service account and a small test cluster or you can use our dedicated trial env — whichever you prefer. We'll be explicit about least privilege.
[06:10] Maya: Security: we need SSO, RBAC, and user audit trails. Are these supported out of the box?
[06:15] Sofia: Yes — SSO via SAML/OIDC, role-based access controls, and audit logs. We'll include a security pack doc.
[06:22] Maya: Great. Any competitors we should consider? We looked at MegaCloudAI and also considered building more in-house.
[06:29] Sofia: Right — MegaCloudAI has an easy entry but usually costs more at scale. Building in-house gives control but ops overhead. Redwood aims to give middle ground: you get serving optimizations and routing controls without full ops burden.
[06:41] Jordan: Pricing sensitivity — can you show a model where we keep a small critical route on a high-SLA pool and everything else on a cheaper batch pool? We want to see blended unit cost.
[06:51] Ravi: Absolutely — that's a standard approach. We'll include a blended cost view in the spreadsheet and a routing config example.
[07:00] Maya: One more question — on billing, do you report token-level breakdowns per route so product owners can see which features burn most tokens?
[07:08] Sofia: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route token/latency/cost dashboards and exportable reports.
[07:15] Samir: Okay next steps?
[07:18] Sofia: Recap. We'll: 1) Sofia send pricing tiers and pilot agreement; 2) Ravi prepare perf/cost estimate and benchmark plan; 3) Jordan provide sample payloads and token distribution; 4) schedule a benchmark slot. Anything else?
[07:34] Maya: Please include a clear comparison table for hosted vs dedicated vs private with unit costs and control/security tradeoffs.
[07:40] Sofia: Will do.
[07:42] Samir: timeline — we want the pilot run within two weeks if possible.
[07:46] Sofia: We'll aim to start benchmarks by 2026-06-10.
[07:50] Jordan: Noted. I'll get the sample CSV to you tomorrow.
[07:53] Sofia: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with the docs and pricing.

End of transcript.

References shared: Redwood pilot pricing doc (link shared in chat), Security pack (link), sample benchmark template (link)
